clue.text: Rope fibre from lasso cut and spun, catching setter

indicators.note: a word that is cut loses its tail, so its final letter goes
something spun round faces the other way, so the shortened word is read backwards
the turned word catches the setter, holding that piece inside itself

blocks.note: lasso without its last letter
the setter refers to themself as I

explanation.surface: A cowboy's rope is made by cutting and twisting a lasso, with the setter caught up in it.
explanation.walkthrough: LASS reversed is SSAL, and the setter's I goes in after the first S to make SISAL.
explanation.definitionFit: Sisal is a stiff plant fibre from an agave, traditionally twisted into rope and twine.

clue.text: Pastor meekly suppresses outburst

indicators.note: the two words suppress, or hold down inside them, the answer across their join

blocks.note: letters running across the two words

explanation.surface: A mild-mannered clergyman quietly holds back an angry outburst.
explanation.definitionFit: A storm can mean a violent outburst of feeling, such as a storm of protest.

clue.text: That woman will try to find out what's in Molly Malone's wheelbarrow

blocks.note: she'll, short for she will
to fish is to probe for information

explanation.surface: A curious woman means to discover what Molly Malone is carrying.
explanation.walkthrough: Molly Malone is the Dublin fishmonger of the song, wheeling her barrow and crying 'cockles and mussels'.
explanation.definitionFit: Cockles and mussels, sold from Molly Malone's barrow in the song, are both kinds of shellfish.

clue.text: One standing at the end of a mast, swinging lantern-case around

indicators.note: a word's case is its outside, so only its first and last letters are kept
swinging letters swing about and land in a different order
around has the outer letters enclosing the rearranged phrase

blocks.note: the first and last letters of lantern
the two words as written, ready to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A sailor clings to the top of a mast as a lantern swings round it.
explanation.walkthrough: A MAST rearranged is ASTMA, with L...N around it.
explanation.definitionFit: The last man is the final survivor, the one still on his feet when everyone else has fallen.

clue.text: Talk to me about the Queen's storage unit

indicators.note: about can mean around in a jumbled way, so the two little words are rearranged

blocks.note: to gas is to chatter idly
the two words as written, ready to be rearranged
Elizabeth Regina, the late Queen's cipher

explanation.surface: Someone asks to hear about where the Queen keeps her belongings.
explanation.walkthrough: GAS + OMET (TO ME rearranged) + ER gives GASOMETER. ER, Elizabeth Regina, is the standard crossword Queen.
explanation.definitionFit: A gasometer is a large tank holding town gas, so it is literally a storage container for fuel.

clue.text: Chewed, green rind - a watermelon rind?

indicators.note: the rind is the skin of a fruit, so only the outside letters of each word are kept

blocks.note: the first and last letters of green
taken as written
the first and last letters of watermelon

explanation.surface: Someone has chomped a green watermelon down to its rind.
explanation.walkthrough: The repeated 'rind' signals outer letters twice, once for green and once for watermelon.
explanation.definitionFit: Gnawn is an old past participle of gnaw, meaning bitten or chewed at persistently.

clue.text: Chopping leeks? Loads - you'll find them in the cupboard

definitions.text: you'll find them in the cupboard

indicators.note: chopping cuts the vegetable into bits that can be put back together differently

blocks.note: the word as written, ready to be rearranged
tons of something means loads of it

explanation.surface: A kitchen picture: piles of chopped leeks, the rest stored in the cupboard.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition plays on the idiom of skeletons in the cupboard, meaning hidden secrets; Americans say closet.
explanation.definitionFit: Skeletons in the cupboard are embarrassing secrets kept hidden, so the idiom puts them there.

clue.text: Like a man's overheard secret

indicators.note: overheard means caught by ear, so the sound of the phrase matters rather than its spelling

blocks.note: mister-y, coined as an adjective meaning like a mister, a man

explanation.surface: A man's private secret is accidentally overheard.
explanation.walkthrough: Mister plus the adjective ending -y makes a jokey word for man-like, which sounds the same as the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A mystery is something unknown or kept hidden, so it is a secret.

clue.text: A piece of Baronet Rothschild's upside-down cake

indicators.note: a piece of the following words is cut out from inside them
in a down entry upside-down means reading from bottom to top

blocks.note: letters running across the two words

explanation.surface: A slice of a wealthy baronet's upside-down cake.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Upside-down cake' is a real dessert, so the reversal signal hides in plain sight.
explanation.definitionFit: A torte is a rich, layered continental cake, often made with ground nuts.

clue.text: Strange footnote: 'Tree from which this produce is derived'

definitions.text: Strange footnote: 'Tree from which this produce is derived'

blocks.note: rum means odd or strange
a postscript, a note added at the end
teak is a tropical hardwood tree

explanation.surface: An odd footnote claims to name the tree some produce came from.
explanation.walkthrough: RUM + PS + TEAK. As a whole the clue jokes that the steak is grown on a teak tree, which is plainly strange.
explanation.definitionFit: Rump steak is a cut of beef, meat produce that comes from a cow, not from any tree.

clue.text: Aggrandise Sri Lanka, say, after a brief spell of cricket

indicators.note: after says the cricket piece comes first, with the country example following it

blocks.note: an over is a set of six balls bowled in cricket
Sri Lanka is an example of a nation state

explanation.surface: Someone talks up Sri Lanka after a short stint watching it play cricket.
explanation.walkthrough: 'After' puts the cricket piece first even though the clue names Sri Lanka first. An over is a cricket unit of six balls.
explanation.definitionFit: To overstate is to exaggerate, making something seem bigger or grander than it really is.

clue.text: Go out, laugh, take drugs

indicators.note: take here means take away, and drugs is the usual crossword code for ecstasy, so that drug's letter is removed

blocks.note: something hilarious is a scream, a real laugh

explanation.surface: A wild night instruction: go out, have a laugh and take some drugs.
explanation.walkthrough: SCREAM loses its E (ecstasy) to leave SCRAM. 'Take drugs' reads like partying but means remove the drug.
explanation.definitionFit: Scram is a slangy order to leave at once, the same as telling someone to get out.

clue.text: He delivers knitwear and mohair caps within fashionable Italian city

indicators.note: caps are the tops, so only the opening letter of each garment word is kept
within places the kept letters inside the name of the city

blocks.note: the first letter of knitwear
the first letter of mohair
Milan is Italy's fashion capital

explanation.surface: A courier brings knitwear and mohair hats into Milan's fashion world.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Delivers' suggests parcels of clothing rather than bottles of milk; Milan is the fashion capital of Italy.
explanation.definitionFit: A milkman's job is a daily round bringing milk to people's doorsteps, so he is a deliverer.

clue.text: Sea captain's birds leaving rents or small holes

indicators.note: the birds are leaving, so that word departs from the name of the captain

blocks.note: Captain Birdseye is the bearded sea captain who advertises a British brand of frozen fish fingers
the word as written, the part that departs
lets are properties rented out, or the verb to rent

explanation.surface: Seabirds abandon the tears in a sail, leaving only small holes behind.
explanation.walkthrough: Captain Birdseye is the mascot of a British frozen-food brand; drop BIRDS from BIRDSEYE for EYE, then add LETS. 'Rents' suggests tears, but it means lets.
explanation.definitionFit: Eyelets are little reinforced holes for laces or cords, as in shoes or sails.

clue.text: Exhausted corgi carried by son/heir

indicators.note: an exhausted word is emptied of its insides, so only its outer letters remain
carried by means held inside, so the remnant sits within the next word

blocks.note: the first and last letters of corgi
taken as written

explanation.surface: A tired royal corgi is carried home by the son and heir.
explanation.walkthrough: The slash makes son/heir look like one phrase, but son is wordplay and heir is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A scion is a descendant or heir of a notable family, especially a young one.

clue.text: The antithesis of fast food in France, maybe accompanied by relish

blocks.note: snails, escargots, are a French delicacy
to relish something is to like it

explanation.surface: A French dish served slowly with a sauce on the side, the opposite of fast food.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fast food' and 'relish' suggest burgers and sauce; fast is the definition's adjective, food starts the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Snails are proverbially slow, so moving at a snail's pace is the opposite of quick.

clue.text: Conservative policy is heralded by the commencement of secret plot

indicators.note: the commencement of a word is its opening letter, so only that is kept
being heralded by something means it arrives first, so the kept letter goes in front

blocks.note: the first letter of secret
a Tory is a member of the UK Conservative Party
a party line is its official policy

explanation.surface: A Conservative policy is announced as the start of a secret plot.
explanation.walkthrough: S + TORY + LINE. 'Plot' reads as a conspiracy in the surface; here it is the story of a book or film.
explanation.definitionFit: A storyline is the sequence of events in a narrative, which is the plot.

clue.text: Scrape piece of rock to make screw

blocks.note: to skin a knee is to scrape it
flint is a hard stone

explanation.surface: DIY instructions: scrape a stone to fashion a screw.
explanation.walkthrough: Screw is informal for a miser, someone who screws every penny out of others.
explanation.definitionFit: A skinflint is a mean, stingy person, which is also what the slang word screw can mean.

clue.text: I finally strongarm Italian suspect into sucking a dummy

indicators.note: finally keeps just the final letter of the next word
something sucking takes in what follows, so the lone article is drawn into the word
suspect means dubious, not to be taken at face value, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written
the last letter of strongarm
It is an abbreviation for Italian, as on vermouth
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A tough guy forces an Italian suspect to suck on a baby's dummy.
explanation.walkthrough: A goes into INTO, and that is rearranged to ATION. A dummy is the British word for a baby's pacifier, but here means a fake.
explanation.definitionFit: A dummy is a replica or fake object, so it is an imitation of the real thing.

clue.text: Lithe cats dancing, running and jumping, etc.

indicators.note: dancing letters move about the floor and end up in a new order

blocks.note: the two words as written, ready to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Supple cats leap about, dancing, running and jumping.
explanation.definitionFit: Athletics is the sport made up of track and field events such as races, jumps and throws.

clue.text: They introduce old radio plays

indicators.note: plays means moves about freely, so the letters of the word before are rearranged

blocks.note: ex means former
the word as written, ready to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Classic radio dramas are being introduced to new listeners.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Radio plays' reads as a single genre, but plays is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Exordia, plural of exordium, are the opening parts of speeches or treatises that introduce them.

clue.text: Beginning to loosen, being surrounded by pink noise

indicators.note: the beginning of a word is its first letter, so just that is kept
surrounded means enclosed, so the kept letter goes inside the colour word

blocks.note: the first letter of loosen
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone starts to relax as they are bathed in soothing pink noise.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pink noise' looks like a single sound term, but pink is the container and noise alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A plink is a short, sharp, metallic sound, like a plucked string or a drop hitting tin.

clue.text: Programme that's about peas, and about what's in the middle of whistles

indicators.note: what's in the middle of a word is its central pair of letters, so only those are kept

blocks.note: a pod is what surrounds peas
ca is circa, Latin for about
the two central letters of whistles

explanation.surface: A show about peas and the inside workings of whistles, a quirky programme.
explanation.walkthrough: The repeated 'about' does two jobs: a pod is what is around peas, and ca is about as an abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: A podcast is an audio or video show distributed online, so it is a programme.

clue.text: Nick spoiled the Countdown finale?

blocks.note: to nick or lift something is to steal it
food that has spoiled has gone off

explanation.surface: Someone nicked a contestant's win and ruined the end of Countdown, the long-running British TV word-and-numbers quiz.
explanation.walkthrough: Countdown is a British TV quiz show, but here it is the count before a rocket launches.
explanation.definitionFit: A launch countdown ends at zero with the rocket leaving the pad, which is the moment of liftoff.

clue.text: Yarn created by following expert

blocks.note: f is short for following, as in pp. 5f
an able person is capable, skilled

explanation.surface: Wool spun by a skilled follower of the craft.
explanation.walkthrough: Yarn suggests knitting wool, but here it is a tall tale.
explanation.definitionFit: A yarn is a story, often far-fetched, and a fable is a short moral tale.

clue.text: Mating the desired outcome of this assignment given to whistleblower?

definitions.note: noun phrase for the chess stage in which checkmate is usually delivered

blocks.note: an end is an aim or goal
a referee, who blows the whistle, is assigned a match to officiate

explanation.surface: It suggests a leaker's mission whose aim is some sort of mating, a puzzling scenario.
explanation.walkthrough: The whistleblower is not a leaker but a referee, whose assignment is a match. The question mark flags the loose chess definition.
explanation.definitionFit: In chess the endgame is the final phase, where checkmate is most often achieved.

clue.text: Lament life's end, and the end of masterly, welcoming supporter

indicators.note: the end of a word is its final letter, so just that one is kept from each
welcoming means taking in a guest, so the two kept letters enclose the next piece

blocks.note: the last letter of life
a leg supports a table or a body
the last letter of masterly

explanation.surface: A mournful poem for a life ended, with a master's touch, hosting a supporter.
explanation.walkthrough: E and Y, the two ends, enclose LEG.
explanation.definitionFit: An elegy is a mournful poem written for the dead, a formal lament.

clue.text: Each scrumper thrown out of garden given lines?

blocks.note: Eve took the forbidden fruit and was expelled from Eden
railway lines, abbreviated RY

explanation.surface: Every apple thief caught and expelled from an orchard is made to write lines.
explanation.walkthrough: A scrumper is British slang for someone who steals apples from orchards, and Eve is the original. Lines are a school punishment of repeated sentences.
explanation.definitionFit: Every and each both refer to all members of a group taken one by one.

clue.text: Teddy's here, alongside the tops of ironed new blankets

definitions.text: Teddy's here, alongside the tops of ironed new blankets

indicators.note: the tops of words are their first letters, so one is taken from each of the next three words

blocks.note: the first letters of ironed, new and blankets
Ed is a short form of Edward, as is Teddy

explanation.surface: A child's teddy bear lies tucked up among freshly ironed bedclothes.
explanation.walkthrough: INB + ED. Read as a whole, the clue also describes where the teddy is: tucked under the blankets.
explanation.definitionFit: A teddy lying beside fresh blankets is tucked up for the night, so it is lying between the sheets.

clue.text: It's repetitious nowadays - perhaps one has to be given time

blocks.note: taken as written
the present era is nowadays
T is the abbreviation for time
I've is what one person might say for I have

explanation.surface: It's a tedious modern habit, perhaps: everyone needs to be given time.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One has' becomes the contraction I'VE, as one might say of oneself; 'to be given' sets the time abbreviation in front of it.
explanation.definitionFit: An iterative process repeats the same step again and again, so it is repetitious.

clue.text: Six-footer, 50, wearing 21D with style

indicators.note: the wearer contains what is worn, so the first two pieces go inside the other entry's word

blocks.note: an insect has six feet
L is the Roman numeral for fifty
the answer to 21 Down

explanation.surface: A tall fifty-year-old dresses with flair.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Six-footer' suggests a tall person, but it is an insect with six legs.
explanation.definitionFit: To do something elegantly is to do it gracefully and stylishly.

clue.text: At last, dessert, in a city in Australia - it's a beer

indicators.note: at last points to the final letter of the next word only

blocks.note: the last letter of dessert
taken as written
NY is New York

explanation.surface: After pudding in an Australian city, someone finally gets a beer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In' looks like a placement word, but it is taken literally. A tinny is Australian slang for a can of beer.
explanation.definitionFit: Australians call a can of beer a tinny because it comes in a metal tin.
